content:
Very nice to see the project finally come together :)
Congrats Malvin!

Amazing work! I will definitely have a look, as I am curious how you ended up mechanising cyclic derivations.

Also, do you know how much non-constructivity the proof contains? I know that this is a difficult question to answer in Lean, but maybe you have a rough idea.

Thanks, also for the spot-on question about how constructive it is. The proof we give in the paper is actually constructive in the sense that the tableaux system we give is terminating and that we essentially have an algorithm to compute interpolants from any closed (uniform) tableau. We also have a Haskell implementation of the system that actually computes interpolants.

But the Lean proof at the moment in many places proves an ∃...\exists ...∃... prop where one would actually like to have a function returning a value, including the interpolation result itself. This is mostly because it was easier, not for fundamental reasons. So one possible future project would be to make the Lean implementation more like the Haskell prover, maybe even replacing it fully by also adding a web UI to the Lean project.

(Another non-constructive thing we proved and use is Zermelo's Theorem gamedet, so for a fully constructive proof of the semantic interpolation theorem we might need to have a more powerful version of it.)

(And there are also other noncomputable defs in the project still, coming form docs#Finset.toList but those can also be eliminated via docs#Finset.sort, I just did not manage to make the right instances for that.)

PS: I am happy to answer any more questions too, but maybe we should move to a separate discussion topic if the mods can make one?
3 messages were moved here from #Project announcements > Propositional Dynamic Logic has Craig Interpolation by Chris Henson.

Thanks for the answer!

The pen-and-paper proof was constructive, from what I remember of one of Revantha’s talks. So, all good on that end! :slight_smile:

It would be great to have a constructive proof in Lean indeed, though you’d have to seriously avoid automation if I’m not wrong (due to AC and hence LEM). If you managed to get one, could you then run the code in Lean to compute interpolants, thereby giving you a verified by construction program (unlike the Haskell code, that’s unverified)?

Oh, I did not know you saw the talk by Revantha, nice :)
And I am actually wondering whether there is a middle-ground: suppose we still use automation with AC and LEM to prove that the proof system given by our Tableau type is sound and complete and has interpolation, but then separately write Lean functions to (i) given any valid formula generate a tableau for it and (ii) given any tableau compute the interpolant. If we then show that the functions behave correctly this seems as good as having a constructive proof in the first place? Or would a purist still find this cheating because the proof that the functions behave correctly will still use AC and LEM then?
Maybe my question more generally is whether instead of "extracting code from constructive existence proofs" we can "write code that returns values and prove it's correct"?

That's an interesting idea! I think that a purist could still be unconvinced, as the properties you prove about the function would be established in a non-constructive setting. One that I have in mind, which could be problematic, is termination. Would the functions you have in mind be (constructively?) provably terminating? A critical case I am thinking about is if the function has a LEM baked in deep which cannot be resolved somehow...
